Thoughts on the Unabomber

The Unabomber's essay surprised me. I was expecting a hastily-complied
series of justifications for irrational actions committed purely out
of impulsive anger. I didn't believe that a man who had killed for
reasons that seemed so intuitively unjustifiable could produce
anything resembling sound reasoning. I underestimated him: I found his
manifesto to be a surprisingly intelligent, thought-out accusation of
the potential "evils" of technology.

Which is not to say, however, that I think he is right, logically or
morally. The Unabomber seems to combine two extremely dangerous
elements: he is an excellent psychologist and a poor philosopher. He
points out glaring faults in our society and denounces the corruption
they cause. Unfortunately, his poor reasoning skills lead him to
advocate the incorrect solutions to the problems he perceives.

The Unabomber demonstrates piercing insight into the motivations and
desires of the human mind. I read, for example, his first forty-four
points with great surprise and genuine interest. I personally agreed
with quite a few of the points that he made about the psychology of
20th-century liberalism. His remarks were insightful and objective --
I was almost tempted to commend him for the courage he demonstrated
in daring to attack the irrationality of some aspects of leftism. In
paragraph eighteen, in wh ich he derides leftists for dismissing
"reason, science [!] and objective reality" I wondered how his
manifesto could possibly proceed to advocate an anti-industrial
platform. His reasoning skills leave much to be desired, however, as
he advocates incorrect solutions to the problems he points out,
largely from having accepted incorrect premises. One of his main
errors is the premise that human nature is unchanged from what it was
10,000 years ago. Contemporary society is collapsing because, he
claims, it does not fulfill the needs of "natural" man (by which he
typically means "primitive man"). If human beings had not undergone
any psychological changes since the dawn of civilization, his point
would be valid. However, what was good for man 10,000 years ago is not
necessarily what is good for him now. In this essay, I shall address
some of the Unabomber's key points, and attempt to refute them as best
I can.

The Unabomber's main argument seems to be the following: every human
being needs to go through the "power process," which consists in
pursuing and achieving certain goals of his choice. A significant
aspect of the power process is a poorly-defined concept which he
calls "autonomy," a sort of self-sufficient method of sustaining life
("freedom means being in control of the life-and-death issues of one's
existence: food, clothing, shelter and defense..." [paragraph 84]).
Contemporary society, he claims, robs people of their autonomy by
virtue of its inter-connectivity. Men can no longer survive
independently: we are necessarily forced into contact with others by
the nature of our society (which is determined by advancing
technology). We depend on othe rs for our jobs, for our food, and for
our shelter. This lack of self-sufficiency, this sensation of being
but a "single cog in the machine" is what the Unabomber claims has
caused the widespread psychological problems in our culture, and is
what will, in time, cause its collapse. This particular problem has
arisen only recently because, previously, men took care of their basic
biological needs by themselves or in small communities. Now, because
of technology, we work as an anonymous part of some enormous
corporation, we buy pre-packaged meat for consumption, and we can turn
on the air-conditioner when it's too warm out. Because we do not care
for these needs ourselves, we become psychologically frustrated, and
this frustration is the root of our current social decline.

I believe that the error in his reasoning is the following: human
needs are not static with time. As human beings evolve, human needs
evolve. It may have once been psychologically beneficial for primitive
man to hunt and kill his own meat, but I fail to see why this must be
the case now. Although I do agree that human beings need a certain
sense of fulfillment, and that a portion of this fulfillment must be
attained by the individual's own effort (see Maslow's theory of
needs), I do not think that simple biological needs are still
included in this category. Advancing in one's profession, for example,
can more than adequately serve this human drive. Creation and
invention have been described as some of the most fulfilling of human
experiences (and often occur in conjunction with technological
research. Thus, it is perhaps this very drive which is the motivating
force behind technology.)

The Unabomber also lists several supplementary points describing the
negative effect of technology upon man: these points can be dealt with
collectively, and are: increased population density, isolation of man
from nature, rapidity of social change, and the breakdown of
small-scale communities. All of these, he claims, are contributing to
modem man's increased stress, aggression and perversion.

My response to this point is the same as my previous one: the
Unabomber apparently assumes that because human beings have always had
a certain element in their environment, they are necessarily dependent
upon it. He seems to ignore the fact that human beings evolve and
adjust psychologically to their surroundings. The four points named
above have only affected the past two generations, and human nature
seems already to have adjusted: the trend can only be expected to
continue in the future. Place a small-town farmed in New York, and
place a native New Yorker in a farm, and both will feel stressed
because both are accustomed to their own environment.

Another reason that he cites for modem man's sensation of impotence is
our lack of decision-making power. Because we live in a society of
millions of people, each individual's voice is rendered insignificant.
The majority of decisions in the average person's life (political,
economical, judicial, ecological, military, etc.) are determined by
people other than himself He feels trapped, meaningless,
unappreciated. If technology were dismantled, human beings would live
in small autonomous social units in which the individual would have
significant decision-making power.

The Unabomber here seems to be grasping onto a 19th-century
romanticized version of primitive life. He assumes that human beings
had more freedom and more autonomy in the past than they do now, which
is demonstrably false. European civilization since the dawn of
Christianity up to the 17th century has been almost wholly feudal.
Rather than a citizen who had one one-millionth of the say in the
activities of the government, the average human being was a land-bound
peasant who had none. He was a slave, without any human dignity or
self-sufficiency. Even after the fall of feudalism, social structures
still subjugated the majority to a powerful minority. The Unabomber
fails to recognize a basic premise of history: human beings have
always been dependent upon other human beings, the vast majority of
them never experiencing any sense of autonomy in all their lives. Even
the smaller social units (baronies, villages) have always been
subjugated to the larger ones (duchies, kingdoms), so the Unabomber's
romanticization of small autonomous social groups is similarly
unfounded. The development of democracy is one of the first times in
history that all members of a social group have been given any power
at all.

While the Unabomber is typically an insightful psychologist, he makes
one claim in particular which surprised me in its lack of depth: that
it is contrary to human nature to be interested in science ("Most
scientists work on ... problems that are not the object of normal
curiosity" [paragraph 87]). He claims that no scientist works out of
interest in the field: science is only a "surrogate activity" to
satisfy his drive for power. Nobody who is merely "interested" in his
field could spend as much time in it as do scientists. And since
science controls society, all human beings are simply means to the end
of the psychological needs of scientists. Furthermore, he claims that
we are corrupting childrens' childhoods by forcing them to study
science (beca use society demands that there be more scientists). "It
isn't natural for an adolescent human being to spend the bulk of his
time sitting at a desk absorbed in study. A normal adolescent wants to
spend his time in contact with the real world." [Paragraph 115]

Again, his error seems to lie in the assumption behind the term
"normal," which the Unabomber equates with "primitive." Human
interests change with time, with the evolution of society, and with
the evolution of man's brain. I can personally attest that many
scientific matters interest me in and of themselves, and one wonders
how such thinkers as Einstein, Fermi and Galelio could possibly have
achieved such momentous accomplishments if they had been motivated by
some force other than curiosity (certainly not the personal power
drive, at least in the case of Galileo, who was condemned as a heretic
for his work). Another one of the major philosophical flaws I see in
the Unabomber's manifesto is his view of society. He often speaks of
"the system" in reference to our social structure. He refers to it as
a separate, malevolent entity which bends individuals to its will. It
does so through brainwashing (school indoctrination of the sciences)
and coercion (police forces). He speaks of "the system" as if its
goals were different than those of individuals who compose it. It is
"the system" which needs more scientists, and it is "the system"
which benefits from technology, and it is "the system" which forces
people to conform. "The system" offers individuals an ephemeral,
superficial security in return for the right to do as it pleases with
them.

But what is "The system" other than a group of individuals? It is
individuals who benefit from technology, individuals who teach science
and individuals who enforce laws. Speaking of society as a whole
(whether it's called "society" or "the system" or "the establishment")
may be a semantically useful method of referring to a group of people,
but it must not be confused with an actual separate entity with goals
apart from the individuals who constitute it. The Unabomber blurs this
distinction, and uses this terminological vagueness to his advantage.
And in response to the loss of some human rights: human beings do give
up certain rights in order to remain part of a democratic society:
this is political ideology of John Locke, the theorist behind most of
Western civilization: one renounces certain rights in order to gain
other benefits. If an individual chooses not to enter into the social
contract, he is not legally obliged to participate and is free to
leave the country.

Finally, enumerating the benefits of technology seems unnecessary and
I won't waste space describing the innumerable ways in which it
increases our standard of living today. I will, however, point out
that the advancement of technology has invariably caused and
accompanied advancements in the arts, the social and political
sciences and philosophy. It has continually raised the standard of
living and helped equalize the different class structures (for
knowledge is accessible to anyone who can read, bourgeois or
aristocrat). When technological advancement wanes, the human condition
wanes (the Dark Ages, for example); when technological innovation
flourishes, the human condition flourishes (ancient Greece). In fact,
it is difficult to cite any element in history that has had a more
consistently beneficial effect than technology.

The Unabomber puts up a good rhetorical fight, but I find his
conception of human nature too static and too limiting for his main
arguments to persuade me. I must admit, however, as with any
intellectual sparring partner, that I respect his intellect an d his
insights into human nature. He remarked in his Manifesto "in order to
get our message before the public with some change of making a lasting
impression, we've had to kill people." Although I certainly don't
approve of his method, I find it equally sad that the American public
is so deaf to new intellectual ideas that he felt the need to use
violence simply to gain an audience.
